entry.title: Welcome To My New Website
entry.content:
Welcome! This site collects my research on gravitational-wave cosmology, my publications, and occasional articles — some technical, some written for anyone curious about what gravitational waves can tell us about the Universe.

If you are new to the topic, start with the research page, which gives a ten-line overview and links to the main topics I work on. If you are looking for a specific paper, the publications page has a curated top three and a complete list that stays in sync with INSPIRE-HEP automatically.

And if you find a cat somewhere on this website: yes, that is intentional. Try clicking on it.

entry.title: What Is The Gravitational-Wave Background?
entry.content:
Imagine standing in the middle of a stadium during a match. You cannot make out any single conversation, but you clearly hear the crowd: a continuous, unmistakable hum. The gravitational-wave background is exactly that — the combined “sound” of countless black hole and neutron star mergers, too faint and too numerous to be heard one by one.

Adding An Image

Adding a picture to a post takes one line. Put the image file in the assets/img/ folder and include it like this:

Captions like this one are added with a simple "caption" block. PROXY: replace with a real figure.

Adding Equations

Equations work out of the box, written in standard LaTeX. Inline math like \(h_c \sim 10^{-25}\) flows with the text, while displayed equations get their own line:

\[\Omega_{\rm GW}(f) = \frac{1}{\rho_c} \frac{d\rho_{\rm GW}}{d\ln f}\]

This quantity — the energy density of gravitational waves per logarithmic frequency interval — is the main character of the field: measuring how it depends on frequency \(f\) and on the direction in the sky tells us where the hum comes from.

Why It Matters

The background carries information no single merger can provide: it knows about all the sources, including those far too distant to detect individually, and about the structure of the Universe the signal traveled through. Listening to the crowd, not just the loudest fans, is how we will learn the demographics of black holes across cosmic history.
